subtitle: The sword half-drawn, the sea prayed to, the war abandoned

restraint.author: Homer
restraint.locator: Iliad 1, Athena restrains Achilles; Book 1, normalized characters 9293-10273
restraint.excerpt: The son of Peleus was furious, and his heart within his shaggy breast was divided whether to draw his sword, push the others aside, and kill the son of Atreus, or to restrain himself and check his anger. While he was thus in two minds, and was drawing his mighty sword from its scabbard, Minerva came down from heaven (for Juno had sent her in the love she bore to them both), and seized the son of Peleus by his yellow hair, visible to him alone, for of the others no man could see her. Achilles turned in amaze, and by the fire that flashed from her eyes at once knew that she was Minerva. “Why are you here,” said he, “daughter of aegis-bearing Jove? To see the pride of Agamemnon, son of Atreus? Let me tell you—and it shall surely be—he shall pay for this insolence with his life.” And Minerva said, “I come from heaven, if you will hear me, to bid you stay your anger. Juno has sent me, who cares for both of you alike. Cease, then, this brawling, and do not draw your sword

aftermath.author: Homer
aftermath.locator: Iliad 1, Achilles appeals to Thetis; Book 1, normalized characters 17110-17588
aftermath.excerpt: Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea, weeping and looking out upon the boundless waste of waters. He raised his hands in prayer to his immortal mother, “Mother,” he cried, “you bore me doomed to live but for a little season; surely Jove, who thunders from Olympus, might have made that little glorious. It is not so. Agamemnon, son of Atreus, has done me dishonour, and has robbed me of my prize by force.” As he spoke he wept aloud, and his mother heard him

narrativeBlocks.title: Briseis is taken
narrativeBlocks.body: Agamemnon sends heralds to Achilles's tent and they lead away Briseis — his honour-prize, publicly stripped. Achilles does not stop them; his rage is beyond the point where stopping anyone would satisfy it.

narrativeBlocks.title: The half-drawn sword
narrativeBlocks.body: His heart is divided — draw the sword and kill the king on the spot, or swallow the insult. Athena herself descends, visible to him alone, seizes his hair and holds him back: restrain yourself, and the gods will repay this insult threefold.

narrativeBlocks.title: Weeping by the grey sea
narrativeBlocks.body: Achilles walks alone to the shore and weeps over the boundless water. He is the greatest fighter alive, and the army's commander has just shamed him before everyone — this is not pique, it is a broken compact between leader and warrior.

narrativeBlocks.title: Thetis carries the request
narrativeBlocks.body: His goddess mother rises from the sea to comfort him, and he asks the unthinkable: go to Zeus and beg him to let the TROJANS win. Let the Greeks bleed until they understand what Achilles was worth to them.

narrativeBlocks.title: Rage as the epic's engine
narrativeBlocks.body: The Iliad's first word is 'anger' — menin, a word for divine rage. Achilles's withdrawal is not sulking; it is a god-backed curse on his own side, and Zeus will grant it.

quiz.prompt: What does Achilles ask Thetis to beg of Zeus?

choices.text: That the Trojans prevail in battle — so the Greeks suffer until they feel his worth
That Agamemnon be struck dead in the night
That Briseis be returned by divine command
That he be allowed to sail home to Phthia immediately

quiz.explanation: Achilles asks Zeus to favour the Trojans — the Greeks' own suffering will prove how much they needed him, and it nearly destroys their army.

quiz.prompt: What stops Achilles from killing Agamemnon on the spot?

choices.text: Athena descends, seizes his hair, and orders restraint — promising the insult will be repaid threefold
Nestor talks him down before the army
He decides killing a king would break the oath

quiz.explanation: Athena, visible only to Achilles, holds him back and promises the gods will repay the insult threefold.
